tasks.objective: Establish the true onset and blast radius. Determine the exact minute order-service quote timeouts and pricing-engine p99 rise began (compare 11:30-13:59 window), and check whether other services calling market-data-service or the same downstreams show latency/error degradation at the same time. Report error signatures in order-service logs and whether the timeouts are client-side (waiting on a dependency) or internal (CPU/GC/pool exhaustion). Also report resource trends (CPU, memory, connections) for order-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service.
tasks.answer: Onset is ~12:02-12:06Z (not 12:16Z as reported): pricing-engine p99 jumped in the 12:02 bucket (avg 677.61ms, max 2534.9ms) and saturated at ~2600ms from 12:06; order-service error_rate jumped from ~0.2% to 8.1% in the same 12:06 bucket. order-service ERROR logs are exclusively client-side "pricing-engine quote call timed out after 2500ms" (first at 12:06:10Z), driven by pricing-engine's own internal saturation (CPU ~99-100%, GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo taking 5-9s vs 2s budget), not by market-data-service, which stayed healthy (p99 flat ~40ms).

tasks.objective: Enumerate everything that changed near the incident window across ALL services, not just market-data-service: list deployments and config changes between 11:30 and 13:59, including market-data-service's serialization change and any config/flag changes to order-service or pricing-engine. Map service dependencies to identify shared components between order-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service, and search historical incidents for prior occurrence of quote timeouts / serialization-change-induced latency.
tasks.answer: Between 11:30 and 13:59 only one deployment shipped anywhere (market-data-service v5.2.0 protobuf quote serialization at 11:56Z, still live/not rolled back), and the only config/flag change found is pricing-engine's cfg-3120 raising flags.pricing.greeks_v2.rollout_pct 5->100 at 12:04Z. Order-service had no config changes; pricing-engine had no deploy. Topology: order-service -> pricing-engine -> market-data-service (all http), with shared components ledger-db (order-service, db), redis-cache (pricing-engine, cache) and kafka (order-service, queue) — so market-data-service and order-service share no direct datastore. Prior similar-symptom incidents were caused by cache/redis failover (HIST-107), pricing-engine CPU saturation (HIST-113) and ledger-db IOPS throttling (HIST-110), i.e. quote-timeout symptoms have multiple unrelated historical causes.

tasks.objective: Task a's onset time is known; use it to correlate. For the specific candidate change(s) identified by task b (market-data-service serialization change and any other change within ~15 min of onset), check pre/post metrics: did p99 latency for pricing-engine's calls to market-data-service, the market-data-service request rate/payload size, and market-data-service CPU/error rate shift exactly at the deploy step? Determine whether the market-data-service payload size/latency increased after the serialization change versus whether an unrelated downstream component degraded at the same time.
tasks.answer: No: the market-data-service serialization change (dep-6111, v5.2.0 protobuf, 11:56Z) produced no metric shift at the deploy step. market-data-service's latency_p99 stayed flat ~39-41ms (min 35.28/max 43.75), request_rate stayed ~940 req/s, cpu_pct ~45%, and error_rate ~0.2% across 11:30-13:59Z, including the 12:02-12:06 onset buckets. The degradation is instead local to pricing-engine: its CPU pinned to ~99% and latency saturated at ~2600ms from 12:02-12:06Z while its own request_rate (~645 req/s) and memory_pct (~49%) stayed flat, pointing at a pricing-engine-local change (the cfg-3120 greeks_v2 rollout 5->100 at 12:04Z sits closest to onset, with CPU already rising in the 12:02 bucket) rather than any payload/latency increase in market-data-service.

Alternatives H2/H4 are properly contradicted by flat mds and pricing-engine metrics; H3/H5 remain untested rather than refuted (redis-cache and other-service config changes were never queried, and the global config audit was partial per F6). However, H1's causal chain has a temporal weak point that is currently unresolved: pricing-engine CPU and latency already began rising in the 12:02 bucket (F9/F10), which is BEFORE the 12:04Z cfg-3120 timestamp. The flagged bucket-boundary/timestamp-skew explanation is an assumption, and no bucket-level trace between 11:56Z and 12:04Z was produced to show whether the pricing-engine step coincides with the flag ramp or precedes it. That is a blocking-evidence gap for the specific causal claim. Because the decisive separating query is obtainable (bucket-level pricing-engine CPU/latency at 11:56/11:58/12:00/12:02/12:04/12:06, plus redis-cache metrics to test H3), the correct verdict is needs_evidence, not inconclusive. H1 is very likely correct, but I would not defend >0.62 confidence until the pre-ramp buckets and the redis-cache alternative are resolved.

challenges.issue: Temporal-order gap: pricing-engine CPU/latency already rise in the 12:02 bucket, before the 12:04Z cfg-3120 change timestamp (F9/F10 vs F2). The bucket-boundary/timestamp-skew explanation is listed as an assumption, not verified. If pricing-engine CPU actually begins stepping at 12:02 or earlier, the flag ramp cannot be the proximate driver of the initial degradation, and the causal hop 'cfg-3120 -> GreeksV2 hot path -> CPU saturation' is not tight. No sub-bucket resolution between 11:56Z and 12:04Z was requested.

H3 (redis-cache saturation) is marked 'rejected' but was never tested: redis-cache metrics were never queried (tool budget exhausted). It is dismissed on the argument that a cache slowdown wouldn't produce a GreeksV2-specific signature — which is plausible but is reasoning, not evidence. With F6 showing the config audit was incomplete and F5 citing HIST-107 (redis failover) as a real prior quote-latency cause, an untested shared-cache alternative adjacent to onset is a major gap.

H5 rests on the partial config-audit result (F6, shard 2/3 down) and was never retried. The absence of config changes on redis-cache/kafka/gateways is inferred from an incomplete result, which is exactly the failure mode to avoid. Unlike H3, H5 also has low prior plausibility (no mechanism linking an unqueried-service flag to a pricing-engine-local GreeksV2 signature), so this is major rather than blocking.

H2 is well contradicted (F12-F16, F18) but the rejection leans partly on 'no payload-size metric exists' — the serialization change's payload effect is only excluded by proxy metrics (latency/request_rate/cpu/memory all flat). This is adequate for server-side degradation but is a proxy argument, not a direct measurement. Minor given how uniformly flat mds is.

Blast-radius check is incomplete: only order-service is confirmed as a pricing-engine caller timed out. If no other pricing-engine caller degraded, H1's 'saturated for all traffic' claim is weakened and a caller-specific explanation deserves weight. Not blocking given the internal log signature is pricing-engine-wide, but it is unverified.

evidence_requests.question: Produce bucket-level pricing-engine cpu_pct and latency_p99_ms at every 1-2 minute bucket from 11:54Z through 12:08Z (specifically 11:56, 11:58, 12:00, 12:02, 12:04, 12:06). Determine whether pricing-engine CPU/latency shows a step change exactly at the 12:04Z cfg-3120 flag ramp, or whether the step begins at/before 12:02Z (which would precede the flag change). Report per-bucket averages, not just the 12:02 and 12:06 buckets.
evidence_requests.rationale: This is the blocking gap: H1's causal hop requires the pricing-engine CPU step to coincide with or follow cfg-3120 at 12:04Z, but current evidence shows CPU already rising in the 12:02 bucket. Sub-bucket resolution separates H1 from a cause preceding the flag ramp.

evidence_requests.question: Query redis-cache metrics (cpu_pct, latency, hit/miss rate, memory, connections) across 11:30-13:59Z, focusing on 12:00-12:06Z. Report whether redis-cache shows any degradation coinciding with pricing-engine's 12:02-12:06 CPU/latency saturation.
evidence_requests.rationale: H3 (shared redis-cache saturation) is marked rejected but was never tested because the metric query never ran. Flat redis metrics would actually falsify H3; any degradation would elevate it.

Report any config/flag changes on redis-cache, ledger-db, kafka, api-gateway, or exchange-gateway in-window, or state definitively that the shard is still unavailable.
evidence_requests.rationale: H5 is only excluded by an incomplete (partial=true) result. A clean retry either rules H5 out or surfaces a missed change; if permanently unavailable, that should be recorded so H5 is treated as untestable rather than dismissed.

critiques.summary: H1 is now adequately supported and survives round 2's scrutiny. The round-1 blocking gap — that pricing-engine CPU/latency appeared to begin rising in the 12:02 bucket, BEFORE the 12:04:16Z flag apply — is closed by verified 1-minute-bucket data: CPU (38-42%) and p99 (57-62ms) are flat and indistinguishable from baseline in every bucket through 12:04Z inclusive (12:02 40.08/58.17, 12:03 40.18/56.82, 12:04 38.22/60.53), then step simultaneously in the 12:05 bucket (98.65% / 2534.9ms) with missing_points=0, partial=false (F25-F27, F29-F30). F28 fixes ordering: the cfg-3120 apply logs at 12:04:16Z, the first GreeksV2 Monte-Carlo WARN at 12:05:21Z. So cause precedes effect by one bucket, tightly and completely. The mechanism is corroborated by an internal log signature in pricing-engine itself (Monte-Carlo paths=20000 at 2964-8942ms; 'deadline exceeded ... calculator=GreeksV2', 2000ms budget, matching order-service's 2500ms client timeout), CPU pinning at ~99% while request_rate (~645 req/s) and memory (~49%) stay flat — the signature of per-request compute cost exploding, not load or payload growth (F11, F17, F25). Alternatives are now contradicted by verified data rather than dismissed: H2 (mds protobuf deploy) — every mds signal flat across both 11:56Z deploy and onset, and it precedes onset by 8 min (F12-F16, F18); H3 (redis-cache saturation) — all five exposed redis signals flat at onset with no error/warn logs (F31-F36); H4 (traffic surge) — request_rate flat on both services (F14, F17); H5 (config change on an unqueried service) — the retried global config audit is now complete (partial=false) and returns exactly ONE in-window change, cfg-3120, with redis-cache/ledger-db/kafka/api-gateway/exchange-gateway each individually confirmed at zero (F19-F24). Remaining gaps (per-pod CPU split, sub-minute resolution, order-service log truncation, ledger-db and pricing-engine blast-radius queries) are non-blocking: none can change the ranking, since H1 is the only hypothesis consistent with the pricing-engine-local GreeksV2 log signature plus the pinned-CPU/flat-throughput signature, and no other change existed anywhere in the fleet window. Confidence capped at 0.88 rather than higher because the mechanism is established by correlation plus log signature rather than a controlled revert/canary experiment, and the 'negligible effect at 5% rollout' baseline was never measured.

challenges.issue: The causal hop flag->compute-cost->CPU saturation rests on correlation plus an in-product log signature, not a controlled experiment: no revert/recovery observation (cfg-3120 back to 5%) and no canary reproduction with flat traffic, and no baseline exists for the prior 5% rollout window. Not ranking-changing and not obtainable by a diagnostic query within the incident window (revert is a remediation action), so it caps rather than blocks.

Ospecific mechanism detail unresolved: cpu_pct is a service-level aggregate, so it cannot be told whether the flag ramped all replicas or one pod is pinned. This does not affect origin or ranking — both readings are the same config change — but it leaves the blast-radius shape imprecise.

redis-cache exposes no latency metric (available_metrics: connected_clients, cpu_pct, evictions_per_min, hit_ratio_pct, memory_pct), so cache-side response latency was never measured directly; H3 is falsified on five flat resource/health counters plus absence of error logs rather than on measured cache latency. Residual risk is small given five independent flat signals and no plausible mechanism linking a healthy cache to a pricing-engine-local GreeksV2 compute blowup.

Blast radius is unconfirmed: other pricing-engine callers and other callers of market-data-service were never queried, and order-service's ERROR list was truncated (30 of 225). This affects remediation scope, not root cause — the pricing-engine-local signature already establishes origin.

Payload size (the objective's stated concern for the protobuf change) has no direct metric; it is excluded only by proxy (flat latency, request_rate, cpu, memory on market-data-service). All proxies are uniformly flat across the deploy and onset, so the exclusion is sound but indirect.
